title: Prune+PlumTree -Finding Eviction Sets at Scale
abstract: Finding eviction sets for a large fraction of the cache is an essential preprocessing step for Prime+Probe based cache side-channel attacks. Previous work on this problem reduces it to finding an eviction set for each cache set independently. In a w-way, set-associative cache with s cache sets this approach requires Ω(s 2 w) time. This work introduces the Prune+PlumTree algorithm, which finds eviction sets for any constant fraction of the cache in time O(sw log s), assuming the LRU cache replacement policy. We complement the asymptotic result with tests on current Intel processors, with 16k sets in the Last Level Cache (LLC) and 4 Kbyte memory pages, finding eviction sets for more than 98% of the LLC in 40-63 milliseconds, improving over previous work by two orders of magnitude. Simulating Prune+PlumTree on a standard, i.e. unskewed, randomized cache, mapping addresses to random cache sets, results in finding eviction sets for more than 98% of a 12-way cache with 2 14 sets in less than 7.4 seconds. We further adapt Prune+PlumTree to caches with a random replacement policy based on a novel method to prune a large set of random memory lines to a union of minimal eviction sets in this setting. This variant of Prune+PlumTree runs in time O(sw 2 log s). As a final contribution, we show that Prune+PlumTree for the LRU replacement policy has asymptotically tight running time by proving that any algorithm that maps a constant fraction of the cache runs in time Ω(sw log s). 3754 2024 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Introduction Cache memory is an essential part of modern processors. Its small size and fast access time enable low-cost, effi- cient processing for computational tasks with high spatial and temporal locality. Most modern caches use the set- associative architecture, in which a cache is divided into s sets, and each set includes w cache-lines or ways. A memory line is mapped to a specific set but can be stored in any of the w cache lines. Insertion to a full set leads to an eviction of a resident line as determined by a cache replacement policy. In any multi-processing environment, the small size of cache memory requires its sharing between processes. The timing difference between access to the main memory and to the cache creates a side channel, potentially leaking information across security domains. Prime+Probe [1], [2] is an important type of cache side- channel attack, which can often be used when an attacker process and a victim process are co-located on the same system, and use a shared cache. The attacker primes a cache set by filling it with addresses from its own memory space, waits, and then probes the same addresses. The latency of the probes reveals whether a different process, potentially the victim, accessed memory locations in the interim, evict- ing the attacker's data from the cache. Prime+Probe has been successfully applied to attacking a variety of targets including: extracting cryptographic keys [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], leaking information on user input [6], [7], derandom- izing Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) [8], [9], spying on browsing activity [10], detecting co-residency in cloud environments [11], creating fast cross-core covert channels [12], and constructing templates for cache attacks on general targets [13]. Prime+Probe can also be used as a component in complex attacks that abuse several micro- architectural components [14], [15], [16] reading arbitrary data from a different process, or writing to the memory space of that process. Prime+Probe is generally restricted to the popular in- clusive cache architecture, despite exceptions such as [17]. In an inclusive cache, any address stored in a private cache that is only accessible to the core running the target process is also stored in the shared cache that is accessible to the attacker as well. Conversely, any address that is evicted from the shared cache is also evicted from the private cache. This property ensures that the target's access to an address of interest between the Prime and Probe operations results in an eviction of an attacker's address from the cache. The latency of the attacker's access to its own addresses is therefore closely correlated to the target's access to the target of interest, enabling the side channel. A fundamental object in a Prime+Probe attack is an eviction set of w memory lines that are all congruent, i.e. mapped to the same cache set. Accessing the lines of an eviction set is part of both priming and probing a cache set. Efficiently constructing an eviction set for a single cache set holding a memory line of interest has been the subject of recent work [2], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22]. From the perspective of designing secure caches, these attacks outline how the attacker can obtain some minimal information from the victim. An attack that successfully finds a single eviction set is thus viewed as breaking a cache design. However, from an attacker's perspective, finding a single eviction set is almost always insufficient for a successful 3754 DOI 10.1109/SP54263.2024.00173 Prime+Probe attack. Some attacks naturally require eviction sets for many cache sets, e.g. template attacks [13], which monitor multiple cache sets, or variants of Spectre [15] without shared memory between the attacker and the victim. This second attack translates a byte of memory into one of 256 cache sets and must test them all for activity. However, even when an attack calls for monitoring the activity of a single cache set, such as private key extraction from square- and-multiply implementations of exponentiation in groups [2], [23], finding this set is non-trivial. Typically, the attacker is required to find eviction sets for most of the cache sets and run a profiling phase, checking these sets for activity patterns that match the predicted pattern of the desired target set. As a consequence, virtually any Prime+Probe attack must be preceded by an algorithm that maps the cache, i.e. finds eviction sets for most of the cache sets. We say that an algorithm that takes an input q ∈ (0, 1] and finds eviction sets for a q-fraction of the cache sets, is a cache mapping algorithm. Several factors motivate the study, not only of the fea- sibility, but also the efficiency, of both finding a specific eviction set and of mapping the cache. First, there may only be a restricted time window in which the attacker and the target processes are co-located on the same physical system, e.g. in cloud or web environments. Second, the timer resolution may be too low to reliably distinguish between a cache hit and a cache miss. Such timers, which are common for example in web environments, do not prevent Prime+Probe attacks or eviction set discovery, but they do increase the time required for these actions. The attacker can replace each trial of accessing a set of memory addresses and testing for a cache miss with n such trials, for a parameter n chosen such that the given timer resolution is sufficient to distinguish between n cache hits and n cache misses. However, mapping the cache in this case is longer by a factor of approximately n, making less efficient attacks infeasible in practice. Finally, some proposals for securing future cache designs, e.g. [24] specify periodic random refreshing of the mapping between main memory addresses and cache sets, limiting the time in which a cache mapping is correct and useful for a Prime+Probe attack. The complexity measure we use to assess the efficiency of finding eviction sets and mapping the cache is the number of lines that the code accesses. This measure is a worst-case estimate for the number of cache misses, which dominates the running time of the algorithm. Related work. Finding a single eviction set was pioneered by Liu et al. [2] which tests each of O(sw) memory lines for inclusion in an eviction set by accessing all other lines in the set and measuring the latency. The algorithm runs in quadratic time in the cache size or O(s2w2). Subsequent work improved to O(sw3) in the group elimination algo- rithms of [18], [19], which remove a large fraction of the candidate lines before testing the latency of accessing the rest. The next development was O(sw2) memory accesses in the improved group elimination algorithm of [20], and the hierarchy-based algorithm of [21], [25], which requires that the mapped cache has a private, lower level cache. Finally, the complexity was improved to O(sw) in the Prime+Prune+Probe approach of [22]. This body of previous work reduced cache mapping to the problem of finding a single eviction set. Beginning with a sufficiently large set A of random addresses, find an eviction set for a random cache set S, filter from A all addresses that are mapped to S, and repeat until A is empty. Using the asymptotically best algorithm to find a single eviction set in this reduction results in a cache mapping algorithm that runs in O(s2w) time. Our first contribution is the Prune+PlumTree algorithm, which is a cache mapping algorithm for caches with a Least Recently Used (LRU) replacement policy that runs in O(sw log s) time. At a high level, the algorithm first prunes [22], [26] a large collection of random memory lines, called the candidates, into a union of minimal eviction sets. It then creates a tree structure with the pruned candidates at the root, and the individual eviction sets at the leaves. In each step, the algorithm uses a second set of random lines, the representatives to iteratively partition collections of minimal eviction sets into smaller collections until individual eviction sets are extracted. This variant of Prune+PlumTree heavily relies on the cache having the LRU replacement policy. We next consider an adaptation to different replacement policies. Specifically, we develop a variant of Prune+PlumTree for the random replacement policy in which an insertion into a full cache set evicts a random line. We design an algorithm for creating a union of many minimal eviction sets that all reside in the cache concurrently. We use it to adapt both the pruning phase and the tree creation phase of the Prune+PlumTree algorithm. The expected running time of this variant is O(sw2 log s). We evaluate the performance of the two variants of Prune+PlumTree both analytically, and by using a simu- lation. These variants are not evaluated directly on a real cache, since all the commercially available CPUs that we are aware of have caches with replacement policies that are neither pure LRU nor purely random. The next contribution of this work is to adapt Prune+PlumTree to run on widely available CPUs and compare it with two other cache mapping algorithms: the group elimination approach of [18], and the hierarchy-based algorithm of [21]. The comparison is on the Last Level Cache (LLC) of three Intel processors of the Whiskey Lake, Coffee Lake, and Comet Lake families with a number of cores that is a power of two, and with a memory space that is divided into regular 4 Kbyte memory pages. It is known that for Intel processors with a number of cores that is a power of 2 [2], [18], [27] if a memory page holds m memory lines then the first memory lines in all the pages are stored in 1/m of the cache sets. Furthermore, given an eviction set for the cache set that holds a line in a memory page, finding eviction sets for the cache sets that hold all other lines in the memory page is immediate. Previous work on this problem reduces it to finding an eviction set for each cache set independently. In a w-way, set-associative cache with s cache sets this approach requires Ω(s 2 w) time. This work introduces the Prune+PlumTree algorithm, which finds eviction sets for any constant fraction of the cache in time O(sw log s), assuming the LRU cache replacement policy. We complement the asymptotic result with tests on current Intel processors, with 16k sets in the Last Level Cache (LLC) and 4 Kbyte memory pages, finding eviction sets for more than 98% of the LLC in 40-63 milliseconds, improving over previous work by two orders of magnitude. Simulating Prune+PlumTree on a standard, i.e. unskewed, randomized cache, mapping addresses to random cache sets, results in finding eviction sets for more than 98% of a 12-way cache with 2 14 sets in less than 7.4 seconds. We further adapt Prune+PlumTree to caches with a random replacement policy based on a novel method to prune a large set of random memory lines to a union of minimal eviction sets in this setting. This variant of Prune+PlumTree runs in time O(sw 2 log s). As a final contribution, we show that Prune+PlumTree for the LRU replacement policy has asymptotically tight running time by proving that any algorithm that maps a constant fraction of the cache runs in time Ω(sw log s). 3754 2024 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)
